Right to History: A Sovereignty Kernel
for Verifiable AI Agent Execution

Jing Zhang Affiliation: Independent Researcher Affiliation: PunkGo Project (https://punkgo.ai) Email: feijiu@punkgo.ai
February 2026
Abstract

AI agents increasingly act on behalf of humans, yet no existing system provides a tamper-evident, independently verifiable record of what they did. As regulations such as the EU AI Act begin mandating automatic logging for high-risk AI systems, this gap carries concrete consequences—especially for agents running on personal hardware, where no centralized provider controls the log. Extending Floridi’s informational rights framework from data about individuals to actions performed on their behalf, this paper proposes the Right to History: the principle that individuals are entitled to a complete, verifiable record of every AI agent action on their own hardware. The paper formalizes this principle through five system invariants with structured proof sketches, and implements it in PunkGo, a Rust sovereignty kernel that unifies RFC 6962 Merkle tree audit logs, capability-based isolation, energy-budget governance, and a human-approval mechanism. Adversarial testing confirms all five invariants hold. Performance evaluation shows sub-1.3 ms median action latency, ∼\sim400 actions/sec throughput, and 448-byte Merkle inclusion proofs at 10,000 log entries.

1 Introduction

AI agents are executing an expanding range of actions on behalf of humans: sending emails, modifying files, running code, calling external APIs. Yet no system today can produce a cryptographic proof of what was done, who authorized it, and whether the agent stayed within its declared bounds. OS-level audit mechanisms (auditd, eBPF tracing) operate at syscall granularity and cannot attribute actions to agent-level semantics or support human-in-the-loop governance; transparent log systems (Certificate Transparency [3], Trillian [32]) provide the cryptographic tooling but have never been applied to agent action recording. As regulations such as the EU AI Act [28] and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework [31] begin mandating automatic logging and transparency for high-risk AI systems, this absence of verifiable agent history is no longer merely a design gap—it is a regulatory liability.

The problem is especially acute when AI agents run on personal hardware. Current regulatory frameworks implicitly assume a centralized provider controlling a log server; when users run agents on their own machines, there is no cloud, no provider, no centralized log. Who guarantees that records exist, are complete, and have not been tampered with?

This paper argues that this constitutes a missing right. Floridi’s information ethics framework [29] establishes that informational entities possess rights related to the creation, processing, and use of information about them—rights that existing legal instruments have begun to codify through data access and transparency obligations [30, 28]. This paper extends this line of reasoning from data about individuals to computational actions performed on their behalf: if individuals have a right to access data held about them, they should equally have a right to access a verifiable record of what AI agents did on their behalf. The Right to History is the principle asserting that individuals are entitled, on their own hardware, to a complete, verifiable, tamper-evident record of every AI agent action—not an optional feature but an architectural commitment that shapes the system’s structure.

Existing work touches different facets of this problem but none provides a complete answer. Agent Contracts [1] formalize what an agent is allowed to do—but do not record what it actually did. AIOS [2] builds an agent operating system—but places the Large Language Model (LLM), rather than a verified kernel, as the trusted computing base (TCB), and provides no audit log. Certificate Transparency [3] demonstrates that Merkle tree append-only logs can protect billions of TLS certificates—but has never been applied to AI agent actions. seL4 [4] proves that an OS kernel can formally verify capability isolation—but does not record what happens within those isolation boundaries.

This paper presents PunkGo, a sovereignty kernel that fills the gap between these bodies of work. The contributions are:

C1. Formal Framework.

A formal model for AI agent action auditing comprising three primitives (Actor, Energy, State), four atomic actions (observe, create, mutate, execute), and five system invariants (Append-Only, Completeness, Integrity, Boundary Enforcement, Energy Conservation), with proof sketches for each invariant following a structured pre-/post-condition argument style. Unlike Agent Contracts [1], which specify what agents may do, this framework argues that what agents actually did is completely recorded and tamper-evident.

C2. PunkGo Kernel.

A Rust implementation that unifies RFC 6962-style Merkle tree audit logs, capability-based writable-target boundaries, and energy budget governance (including a hold_on human-approval mechanism) within a kernel-level TCB. Unlike AIOS [2], which places the LLM as TCB, PunkGo places a verified kernel as TCB.

C3. Sovereignty Inversion.

A directional asymmetry in the AI sovereignty literature: existing work asks how agents maintain sovereignty from humans [5]; the complementary question—how humans maintain sovereignty over agents—has received less attention. The Right to History addresses the latter.

C4. Proof-of-Concept Validation.

Invariant satisfiability is verified on the implemented kernel and key performance characteristics are measured: sub-1.3 ms median action latency, ∼\sim400 actions/sec throughput, and 448-byte Merkle inclusion proofs at 10,000 log entries.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. §2 provides background and motivation. §3 defines the threat model. §4 presents the formal framework (core contribution). §5 describes the system design. §6 reports evaluation results. §7 discusses related work. §8 addresses limitations and future work. §9 concludes.

2 Background and Motivation

2.1 The Accountability Gap in the Age of AI Agents

AI agents are transitioning from experimental tools to everyday executors. Users delegate file management, communications, external service calls, and even arbitrary code execution to LLM-driven agents. This delegation creates a fundamental accountability problem: when actions are driven by an unpredictable LLM, how can humans always (a) know what happened, (b) prove to third parties what happened, and (c) verify that actions stayed within authorized bounds?

Existing agent frameworks fail to answer this question. AIOS [2] provides agent scheduling and context management, but its access control is a rudimentary permission-group hashmap with no audit log and no cryptographic evidence. LangGraph offers an interrupt() pause mechanism that produces no verifiable history. The OpenAI SDK’s needsApproval flag is a boolean switch with no economic constraint against abuse.

The pattern is clear: academia and industry have built the policy layer but not the evidence layer. Agent Contracts [1] define bounds, AgentSentry [6] generates ephemeral permissions, Governance-as-a-Service [7] enforces runtime policies—but none of these systems produce a persistent, tamper-evident, independently verifiable action record.

2.2 The Transparent Log Paradigm

The cryptographic community has solved a structurally analogous problem. Certificate Transparency (CT) [3] uses Merkle tree append-only logs to protect the TLS certificate ecosystem: every certificate issuance is recorded in a public log, inclusion proofs are O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n), and consistency proofs guarantee that the log has not forked. CT now protects billions of certificates, and its Merkle tree structure has been extended to Key Transparency (CONIKS [8]), Go module mirrors (Trillian), and general-purpose verifiable data structures.

Crosby and Wallach [9] formalized data structures for tamper-evident logging, demonstrating that a log of 80 million events requires only 3 KB of proof. Chun et al.’s Attested Append-Only Memory (A2M) [10] goes further, embedding an append-only primitive in the TCB, allowing PBFT to tolerate 1/21/2 Byzantine faults (the classical bound is 1/31/3) with only ∼\sim4% overhead.

These works establish the paradigm’s feasibility and efficiency. Yet no one has applied the transparent log paradigm to OS-level AI agent action auditing. CT records certificates; CONIKS records keys; PunkGo records agent actions.

2.3 Regulatory Urgency

The EU AI Act [28] creates mandatory demand for auditable AI infrastructure. Article 12 requires that high-risk AI systems “shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (‘logs’)”; Article 14 requires human oversight capability, including the ability to intervene in or interrupt operation; Article 19 specifies a minimum six-month log retention period. Penalties for non-compliance reach 7% of global annual turnover or EUR 35 million. High-risk system requirements become enforceable on August 2, 2026.

However, Article 12 implicitly assumes a centralized provider scenario. For AI agents running on personal hardware—a rapidly growing use case—there is no provider controlling the log. The user simultaneously serves as provider, deployer, and overseer. PunkGo enables individuals to self-comply with Articles 12 and 14, reframing logging from a compliance burden into a user right.

2.4 From Data Sovereignty to Computational History Sovereignty

Existing work on data sovereignty [11, 12] establishes principles for user data ownership—but does not address computational history ownership. You can own your data, but can you prove what an agent did with your data? The Right to History (§1) fills this gap: extending the trajectory from data ownership to action-record ownership. You need not control every agent decision (that is the enemy of efficiency), but you should be entitled to a complete, verifiable, tamper-evident record of every agent action on your hardware.

3 Threat Model and Assumptions

3.1 System Boundary and Trust Model

PunkGo’s trust model places the kernel as the TCB. All other components—including AI agents (LLMs), external tools, and the communication layer—are treated as untrusted.

Inside the TCB (trusted).

The PunkGo Kernel: event log (Merkle tree), energy ledger, boundary checker, payload validator, and audit prover.

Outside the TCB (untrusted).

AI agents (LLM-driven), external tools, client interfaces (remote consoles), and the network communication layer.

Trust Assumptions.

A1 (Kernel Trusted).

The kernel code correctly implements the protocol described in this paper. This is the standard TCB assumption, consistent with the pre-verification premise of seL4 [4]. Rust’s memory safety guarantees eliminate entire vulnerability classes (buffer overflows, use-after-free) without runtime overhead; the implementation uses zero unsafe blocks in the core pipeline. Machine-checked verification (using Verus [13]) is future work.

A2 (Hardware Trusted).

The underlying processor and storage correctly execute instructions and persist data. This assumption can be further strengthened via TEEs (e.g., Intel SGX/TDX), listed as future work.

A3 (Agent Untrusted).

This is the core design premise. LLM-driven agents are non-deterministic, not formally verifiable, and may produce arbitrary output. The entire system design revolves around this point: the design does not trust agent behavior, but trusts the kernel’s record of agent behavior.

A4 (Cryptographic Assumption).

The hash function used (SHA-256) is collision-resistant.

3.2 Adversary Model

The threat model considers five attack scenarios:

T1 (Privilege Escalation).

An agent attempts to operate on targets outside its declared writable_targets—for example, a read-only agent attempting a write.

T2 (Budget Exhaustion).

An agent repeatedly triggers hold_on approvals to lock energy, starving other operations of resources.

T3 (History Tampering).

A compromised non-kernel component (Level 1 adversary) attempts to modify or delete committed events in the log via the kernel API. Direct database manipulation by a root-privileged adversary (Level 2) is outside the current threat model.

T4 (Equivocation / Log Forking).

A compromised component attempts to present different versions of history to different verifiers. Full defense requires external root comparison (see Scope of Defense below and Corollary 4.1).

T5 (Approval Bypass).

An agent attempts to execute high-risk operations without triggering hold_on checks.

Scope of Defense.

It is essential to distinguish two levels of adversary:

Level 1: Untrusted agents (the primary threat). Agents operate as unprivileged actors within the kernel’s jurisdiction. The five invariants (INV-1–5) provide full defense at this level: agents cannot escape capability boundaries, exhaust energy beyond allocation, tamper with committed logs, or bypass human approval. All guarantees in this paper apply to Level 1 adversaries.

Level 2: Privileged platform adversary. A user (or attacker) with root access to the host OS can stop the kernel process, directly modify the underlying storage, and reconstruct the Merkle tree. PunkGo does not currently defend against Level 2 adversaries. Assumptions A1 (kernel trusted) and A2 (hardware trusted) explicitly exclude this case. Defense at Level 2 requires hardware-rooted trust: running the kernel inside a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) such as Intel SGX/TDX, combined with remote attestation and external root anchoring (analogous to Certificate Transparency’s gossip protocol). TEE integration is listed as future work (§8).

This two-level distinction is consistent with systems security practice: seL4 [4] proves isolation properties under analogous TCB assumptions without defending against physical hardware attacks; Certificate Transparency [3] assumes log servers are honest but detects equivocation when they are not, via external gossip—a mechanism PunkGo does not yet implement but whose architectural slot (the Audit Prover’s exported roots) is already in place.

3.3 Security Goals

Table 1 maps each security goal to the threats it addresses and the invariant that provides the guarantee.

4 Formal Framework

This section presents the core theoretical contribution. It first defines the system model (§4.1), then formalizes the event log (§4.2), capability model (§4.3), energy model (§4.4), and hold mechanism (§4.5), and finally states and argues five system invariants (§4.6).

4.1 System Model

Definition 4.1 (World).

A PunkGo system is a triple W=(𝒫,E,S)W=(\mathcal{P},E,S), where 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a finite set of actors, E:𝒫→ℝ≥0E:\mathcal{P}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} is the energy function, and S=(ℒ,W,𝒱)S=(\mathcal{L},W,\mathcal{V}) is the system state comprising the event log ℒ\mathcal{L}, the writability map W:𝒫→2𝑃𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑒𝑟𝑛×𝐴𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑇𝑦𝑝𝑒W:\mathcal{P}\to 2^{\mathit{Pattern}\times\mathit{ActionType}}, and a set of active envelopes 𝒱\mathcal{V}.

Definition 4.2 (Actor Partition).

𝒫=𝒫H∪𝒫A\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}_{H}\cup\mathcal{P}_{A}, where 𝒫H\mathcal{P}_{H} is the set of human actors and 𝒫A\mathcal{P}_{A} is the set of agent actors. 𝒫H∩𝒫A=∅\mathcal{P}_{H}\cap\mathcal{P}_{A}=\emptyset (exhaustive and mutually exclusive).

Axiom 4.1 (Human Unconditional Existence).

∀p∈𝒫H\forall\,p\in\mathcal{P}_{H}: pp cannot be deleted or demoted.

Axiom 4.2 (Agent Conditional Existence).

∀a∈𝒫A\forall\,a\in\mathcal{P}_{A}: aa must declare creator⁡(a)∈𝒫\mathrm{creator}(a)\in\mathcal{P} and purpose⁡(a)\mathrm{purpose}(a) at creation time. creator⁡(a)\mathrm{creator}(a) may set expiry⁡(a)\mathrm{expiry}(a).

Definition 4.3 (Atomic Action).

An action AA is a 5-tuple A=(𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑜𝑟,𝑡𝑦𝑝𝑒,𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡,𝑝𝑎𝑦𝑙𝑜𝑎𝑑,𝑡𝑖𝑚𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑚𝑝)A=(\mathit{actor},\mathit{type},\mathit{target},\mathit{payload},\mathit{timestamp}), where 𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑜𝑟∈𝒫\mathit{actor}\in\mathcal{P}, 𝑡𝑦𝑝𝑒∈{observe,create,mutate,execute}\mathit{type}\in\{\texttt{observe},\texttt{create},\texttt{mutate},\texttt{execute}\}, 𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡∈𝒯\mathit{target}\in\mathcal{T} (the target object identifier), 𝑝𝑎𝑦𝑙𝑜𝑎𝑑\mathit{payload} is the action parameter, and 𝑡𝑖𝑚𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑚𝑝∈ℕ\mathit{timestamp}\in\mathbb{N} (nanoseconds since epoch; the implementation uses 64-bit unsigned integers).

Definition 4.4 (State Transition).

The system advances by actions, not by time:

S′=f⁡(S,A,E)E′=E−cost⁡(A)S^{\prime}=f(S,A,E)\qquad E^{\prime}=E-\mathrm{cost}(A)

where ff is a deterministic state transition function and cost:𝐴𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑇𝑦𝑝𝑒→ℝ≥0\mathrm{cost}:\mathit{ActionType}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}.

Definition 4.5 (Sole Committer).

There exists a unique Committer role κ\kappa responsible for transforming actions into committed events. κ\kappa is a structural role, not a moral authority.

Remark 4.1.

The sole-committer design is deliberate: single-point linearization yields a deterministic total-order log. This aligns with Lamport’s total-order broadcast [14] but simplifies to in-process serialization in the single-machine setting. Multi-committer extension (requiring consensus) is future work.

4.2 Event Log

Definition 4.6 (Event).

An event ee is a tuple e=(𝑖𝑑,𝑠𝑒𝑞,𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑜𝑟,𝑡𝑦𝑝𝑒,𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡,𝑝𝑎𝑦𝑙𝑜𝑎𝑑,𝑝𝑎𝑦𝑙𝑜𝑎𝑑​_​ℎ𝑎𝑠ℎ,𝑡𝑖𝑚𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑚𝑝,𝑎𝑟𝑡𝑖𝑓𝑎𝑐𝑡​_​ℎ𝑎𝑠ℎ,𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑒𝑟𝑣𝑒𝑑​_​𝑒𝑛𝑒𝑟𝑔𝑦,𝑠𝑒𝑡𝑡𝑙𝑒𝑑​_​𝑒𝑛𝑒𝑟𝑔𝑦,𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑛𝑡​_​ℎ𝑎𝑠ℎ)e=(\mathit{id},\mathit{seq},\mathit{actor},\mathit{type},\mathit{target},\mathit{payload},\mathit{payload\_hash},\mathit{timestamp},\mathit{artifact\_hash},\mathit{reserved\_energy},\mathit{settled\_energy},\mathit{event\_hash}), where 𝑖𝑑\mathit{id} is a unique identifier (UUID), 𝑠𝑒𝑞∈ℕ\mathit{seq}\in\mathbb{N} is a monotonically increasing sequence number, 𝑝𝑎𝑦𝑙𝑜𝑎𝑑​_​ℎ𝑎𝑠ℎ=H⁡(canonical⁡(𝑝𝑎𝑦𝑙𝑜𝑎𝑑))\mathit{payload\_hash}=H(\mathrm{canonical}(\mathit{payload})), 𝑎𝑟𝑡𝑖𝑓𝑎𝑐𝑡​_​ℎ𝑎𝑠ℎ\mathit{artifact\_hash} is present for execute actions (echoing the submitted hash), 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑒𝑟𝑣𝑒𝑑​_​𝑒𝑛𝑒𝑟𝑔𝑦\mathit{reserved\_energy} and 𝑠𝑒𝑡𝑡𝑙𝑒𝑑​_​𝑒𝑛𝑒𝑟𝑔𝑦\mathit{settled\_energy} record the energy accounting, and 𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑛𝑡_ℎ𝑎𝑠ℎ=H(0𝚡𝟶𝟶∥canonical(e))\mathit{event\_hash}=H(0\mathtt{x00}\|\mathrm{canonical}(e)) is the RFC 6962 leaf hash.

Remark 4.2.

Inter-event integrity is maintained through the Merkle tree structure rather than per-event hash chains. This is a design choice: Merkle trees provide O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) inclusion and consistency proofs, whereas per-event hash chains support only O⁡(n)O(n) prefix verification. PunkGo uses the Google tlog algorithm (C2SP tlog-checkpoint format), the same structure used by Certificate Transparency and the Go Module Mirror.

Definition 4.7 (Log).

A log ℒ=⟨e1,e2,…,en⟩\mathcal{L}=\langle e_{1},e_{2},\ldots,e_{n}\rangle is a finite totally ordered sequence of events satisfying: (i) ∀i:ei.𝑠𝑒𝑞=i\forall\,i:e_{i}.\mathit{seq}=i (contiguous sequence numbers), and (ii) Merkle tree leaves are ordered by 𝑠𝑒𝑞\mathit{seq}.

Definition 4.8 (Merkle Root).

For a log ℒ\mathcal{L}, its Merkle root is root⁡(ℒ)=MerkleRoot⁡(e1,…,en)\mathrm{root}(\mathcal{L})=\mathrm{MerkleRoot}(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n}), following the RFC 6962 Merkle Hash Tree construction [3].

Definition 4.9 (Inclusion Proof).

For event ei∈ℒe_{i}\in\mathcal{L}, the inclusion proof π⁡(ei,ℒ)\pi(e_{i},\mathcal{L}) is a Merkle path from eie_{i} to root⁡(ℒ)\mathrm{root}(\mathcal{L}), of size O⁡(log⁡|ℒ|)O(\log|\mathcal{L}|). A verifier holding root⁡(ℒ)\mathrm{root}(\mathcal{L}) and π\pi can verify the existence of eie_{i}.

Definition 4.10 (Consistency Proof).

For two log versions ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime} (|ℒ|≤|ℒ′||\mathcal{L}|\leq|\mathcal{L}^{\prime}|), the consistency proof σ⁡(ℒ,ℒ′)\sigma(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}) demonstrates that ℒ\mathcal{L} is a prefix of ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime}, with size O⁡(log⁡|ℒ′|)O(\log|\mathcal{L}^{\prime}|).

4.3 Capability Model

The capability model follows the principle of least privilege, drawing on the foundational capability concept introduced by Dennis and Van Horn [33].

Definition 4.11 (Writable Declaration).

Each actor p∈𝒫p\in\mathcal{P} has a writability set W⁡(p)⊆𝑃𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑒𝑟𝑛×𝐴𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑇𝑦𝑝𝑒W(p)\subseteq\mathit{Pattern}\times\mathit{ActionType}, where 𝑃𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑒𝑟𝑛\mathit{Pattern} is a glob-pattern over target identifiers. W⁡(p)W(p) is declared at the time pp is created.

Axiom 4.3 (Default Deny).

∀\forall action AA by actor pp: if ∄⁡(𝑝𝑎𝑡,𝑡𝑦𝑝𝑒)∈W⁡(p)\nexists\,(\mathit{pat},\mathit{type})\in W(p) such that 𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡⁡(A)∈match⁡(𝑝𝑎𝑡)\mathit{target}(A)\in\mathrm{match}(\mathit{pat}) and 𝑡𝑦𝑝𝑒⁡(A)=𝑡𝑦𝑝𝑒\mathit{type}(A)=\mathit{type}, then AA is rejected.

Definition 4.12 (Root Privilege).

The root actor rr has initial writability W⁡(r)={(**,*)}W(r)=\{(\texttt{**},\texttt{*})\} (full wildcard). Privileged targets (system/*, ledger/*) are writable only by root.

Definition 4.13 (Envelope).

An envelope is a temporary authorization structure ε=(𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑢𝑒𝑟,𝑏𝑢𝑑𝑔𝑒𝑡,𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡𝑠,𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑠,𝑑𝑢𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛,𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑐𝑘𝑝𝑜𝑖𝑛𝑡,ℎ𝑜𝑙𝑑​_​𝑜𝑛,ℎ𝑜𝑙𝑑​_​𝑡𝑖𝑚𝑒𝑜𝑢𝑡)\varepsilon=(\mathit{issuer},\mathit{budget},\mathit{targets},\mathit{actions},\mathit{duration},\mathit{checkpoint},\mathit{hold\_on},\mathit{hold\_timeout}), satisfying 𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡𝑠⁡(ε)×𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑠⁡(ε)⊆W⁡(𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑢𝑒𝑟⁡(ε))\mathit{targets}(\varepsilon)\times\mathit{actions}(\varepsilon)\subseteq W(\mathit{issuer}(\varepsilon)) (the permission subset constraint).

Remark 4.3.

Only human actors (𝒫H\mathcal{P}_{H}) may create agents (enforced by the kernel; agents attempting to create agents receive a policy violation error). However, an agent holding an active envelope may issue a sub-envelope to another existing agent, subject to envelope reduction validation: the sub-envelope’s targets, actions, and budget must be a subset of the issuing envelope’s remaining authorization. This yields a two-tier model: agent creation is human-only, while envelope delegation supports constrained chains with monotonically decreasing privileges.

4.4 Energy Model

The energy model serves two concrete purposes: (1) it provides a denial-of-service defense by limiting each actor’s action rate to a hardware-anchored budget, preventing a single agent from monopolizing the commit pipeline; and (2) it creates an economic constraint on the hold mechanism, ensuring that repeated hold requests have a real cost that deters boundary probing (threat T2). Energy is not a currency to be traded; it is a resource accounting mechanism analogous to process CPU quotas in operating systems, but operating at the semantic action level rather than the instruction level.

Definition 4.14 (Hardware Capacity).

At startup, the kernel reads the hardware compute capacity λ\lambda (measured in INT8 Tera Operations Per Second (TOPS) or a user-configured value) from a configuration file, serving as the physical anchor for energy production.

Definition 4.15 (Continuous Production).

At each tick tt, the system produces energy produce⁡(t)=λ⋅Δ​t\mathrm{produce}(t)=\lambda\cdot\Delta t, where Δ​t\Delta t is the tick duration. The production event is recorded in the log.

Definition 4.16 (Share-Based Allocation).

Each actor pp holds a share share⁡(p)∈ℝ>0\mathrm{share}(p)\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}. Per-tick energy received:

receive⁡(p,t)=share⁡(p)∑q∈𝒫share⁡(q)⋅produce⁡(t)\mathrm{receive}(p,t)=\frac{\mathrm{share}(p)}{\sum_{q\in\mathcal{P}}\mathrm{share}(q)}\cdot\mathrm{produce}(t)
Definition 4.17 (Cost Function).

The cost function cost:𝐴𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑇𝑦𝑝𝑒→ℝ≥0\mathrm{cost}:\mathit{ActionType}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} is a deployment-configurable, monotonically ordered function satisfying: cost⁡(observe)≤cost⁡(create)≤cost⁡(mutate)≤cost⁡(execute)\mathrm{cost}(\texttt{observe})\leq\mathrm{cost}(\texttt{create})\leq\mathrm{cost}(\texttt{mutate})\leq\mathrm{cost}(\texttt{execute}). The execute cost may include an I/O-proportional component based on the output_bytes field reported by the submitting actor.

Remark 4.4.

The reference implementation uses cost⁡(observe)=0\mathrm{cost}(\texttt{observe})=0, cost⁡(create)=10\mathrm{cost}(\texttt{create})=10, cost⁡(mutate)=15\mathrm{cost}(\texttt{mutate})=15, cost⁡(execute)=25+⌊𝑜𝑢𝑡𝑝𝑢𝑡​_​𝑏𝑦𝑡𝑒𝑠/256⌋\mathrm{cost}(\texttt{execute})=25+\lfloor\mathit{output\_bytes}/256\rfloor. These values are derived from profiling the relative pipeline overhead of each action type; the ordering reflects the principle that state-changing actions should cost more than read-only ones. The formal framework is parametric in these values: all invariants hold for any assignment satisfying the monotonicity constraint.

Axiom 4.4 (Production Sufficiency).

λ⋅Δ​t≥max𝑡𝑦𝑝𝑒⁡cost⁡(𝑡𝑦𝑝𝑒)\lambda\cdot\Delta t\geq\max_{\mathit{type}}\,\mathrm{cost}(\mathit{type}), ensuring the Right to History is not undermined by energy design.

Definition 4.18 (Envelope Budget Constraint).

For an active envelope ε\varepsilon: consumed⁡(ε)+reserved⁡(ε)≤budget⁡(ε)\mathrm{consumed}(\varepsilon)+\mathrm{reserved}(\varepsilon)\leq\mathrm{budget}(\varepsilon), where consumed\mathrm{consumed} is settled energy and reserved\mathrm{reserved} is energy locked by pending holds.

4.5 Hold Mechanism

Definition 4.19 (Hold Rules).

An envelope ε\varepsilon may declare hold rules H⁡(ε)⊆𝑃𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑒𝑟𝑛×𝐴𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑇𝑦𝑝𝑒H(\varepsilon)\subseteq\mathit{Pattern}\times\mathit{ActionType}.

Definition 4.20 (Hold Trigger).

When action AA executes under envelope ε\varepsilon and (𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡⁡(A),𝑡𝑦𝑝𝑒⁡(A))(\mathit{target}(A),\mathit{type}(A)) matches H⁡(ε)H(\varepsilon), the kernel atomically: (1) computes cost⁡(A)\mathrm{cost}(A), (2) reserves cost⁡(A)\mathrm{cost}(A) energy, (3) appends a hold_request event to the log, and (4) returns a HoldTriggered status. The envelope remains Active—the agent may continue submitting non-held actions.

Definition 4.21 (Hold Response).

A human actor responds via mutate ledger/hold/⟨id⟩:

  • •

    Approve: execute the original action →\to settle →\to append result event.

  • •

    Reject: settle commitment cost (20%20\% of reserved) →\to release remainder →\to append hold_response event.

  • •

    Timeout (if hold_timeout_secs set): equivalent to reject.

Definition 4.22 (Commitment Cost).

On reject or timeout: commitment​_​cost=⌈0.2×reserved​_​cost⌉\mathrm{commitment\_cost}=\lceil 0.2\times\mathrm{reserved\_cost}\rceil. This reflects hardware resources consumed by validation, quoting, reservation, and recording.

Remark 4.5.

The commitment cost reflects a real resource expenditure: even a rejected or timed-out hold has already consumed kernel resources—validation, quoting, energy reservation, and writing a hold_request event to the append-only log (analogous to reverted transactions still consuming gas in Ethereum). The 20% rate is a configurable engineering parameter balancing two extremes: 0% allows zero-cost boundary probing (enabling T2 budget exhaustion); 100% penalizes legitimate “request-then-approve” workflows. The current value is based on profiling typical agent workloads, where the pre-decision pipeline stages consume approximately 15–25% of total action cost. A formal game-theoretic analysis of the optimal commitment rate under adversarial agent strategies is left as future work.

4.6 System Invariants and Proofs

This section states and argues five core invariants for the PunkGo system. Arguments follow a structured pre-/post-condition style based on the state transition semantics defined in §4.1–§4.5. These are proof sketches rather than machine-checked proofs; full verification using Verus [13] is future work (§8).

Invariant 4.1 (Append-Only).

∀t1<t2\forall\,t_{1}<t_{2}: ℒ⁡(t1)⊑ℒ⁡(t2)\mathcal{L}(t_{1})\sqsubseteq\mathcal{L}(t_{2}), i.e., ℒ⁡(t1)\mathcal{L}(t_{1}) is a prefix of ℒ⁡(t2)\mathcal{L}(t_{2}): ∀i≤|ℒ⁡(t1)|:ℒ⁡(t2)​[i]=ℒ⁡(t1)​[i]\forall\,i\leq|\mathcal{L}(t_{1})|:\mathcal{L}(t_{2})[i]=\mathcal{L}(t_{1})[i].

Proof sketch.

(Step 1) By Definition 4.5, the kernel is the sole committer. The only operation that modifies ℒ\mathcal{L} is Append, whose postcondition is ℒ′=ℒ|⟨e⟩\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}\|\langle e\rangle—concatenation at the end, without modifying existing elements.

(Step 2) No Delete or Modify operation exists in the system. By Axiom 4.3 (default deny), ledger/* targets are writable only by root, and root’s operations also pass through the kernel pipeline, where the only available mutation is Append.

(Step 3) The Merkle tree structure provides additional protection: modifying event eie_{i} changes its leaf hash H(0𝚡𝟶𝟶∥canonical(ei))H(0\mathtt{x00}\|\mathrm{canonical}(e_{i})), invalidating every intermediate node from that leaf to the root. Under the collision-resistance assumption (A4), an attacker cannot find alternative content that preserves the leaf hash.

Therefore ℒ\mathcal{L} grows monotonically. ∎

Invariant 4.2 (Completeness).

∀\forall action AA: if AA passes boundary check (i.e., (𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡⁡(A),𝑡𝑦𝑝𝑒⁡(A))∈W⁡(𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑜𝑟⁡(A))(\mathit{target}(A),\mathit{type}(A))\in W(\mathit{actor}(A))) and has sufficient energy (i.e., passes reserve), then ∃e∈ℒ\exists\,e\in\mathcal{L} recording AA’s commit or hold status.

Proof sketch.

(Step 1) The kernel’s action pipeline is a deterministic linear sequence:

validate→quote→reserve→validate_payload→settle→append→receipt\texttt{validate}\to\texttt{quote}\to\texttt{reserve}\to\texttt{validate\_payload}\to\texttt{settle}\to\texttt{append}\to\texttt{receipt}

(Step 2) Passing boundary check means AA passes validate. Two paths follow: (a) normal path: quote →\to reserve →\to validate_payload →\to settle →\to append; (b) hold path: validate internally performs quote ++ reserve ++ append hold_request →\to HoldTriggered →\to {approve →\to re-submit with replay guards →\to full pipeline →\to append} || {reject/timeout →\to settle commitment →\to append hold_response}.

(Step 3) Both the normal path and the hold path terminate with some form of append. Actions that pass boundary check but lack sufficient energy are rejected at reserve with InsufficientEnergy; these are not recorded in the permanent log, as Energy Conservation (INV-5) takes precedence—the system prioritizes resource integrity over recording resource-denied actions. Completeness thus covers all actions that enter the funded pipeline.

Therefore every boundary-checked, energy-funded action is recorded. ∎

Invariant 4.3 (Integrity).

∀t\forall\,t: root⁡(t)=MerkleRoot⁡(ℒ⁡(t))\mathrm{root}(t)=\mathrm{MerkleRoot}(\mathcal{L}(t)), i.e., the Merkle root precisely commits the current log contents.

Proof sketch.

(Base case) ℒ=⟨⟩\mathcal{L}=\langle\rangle, root=𝑛𝑢𝑙𝑙\mathrm{root}=\mathit{null}. MerkleRoot⁡(⟨⟩)=𝑛𝑢𝑙𝑙\mathrm{MerkleRoot}(\langle\rangle)=\mathit{null}. Holds.

(Inductive step) Assume root⁡(t)=MerkleRoot⁡(ℒ⁡(t))\mathrm{root}(t)=\mathrm{MerkleRoot}(\mathcal{L}(t)). When Append occurs with event ee: ℒ⁡(t+1)=ℒ⁡(t)|⟨e⟩\mathcal{L}(t{+}1)=\mathcal{L}(t)\|\langle e\rangle and root⁡(t+1)=MerkleUpdate⁡(root⁡(t),e)\mathrm{root}(t{+}1)=\mathrm{MerkleUpdate}(\mathrm{root}(t),e). By the correctness of the RFC 6962 Merkle tree construction, MerkleUpdate\mathrm{MerkleUpdate} computes precisely MerkleRoot(ℒ(t)∥⟨e⟩)\mathrm{MerkleRoot}(\mathcal{L}(t)\|\langle e\rangle).

Root is updated only during Append. By INV-1, no other operation modifies ℒ\mathcal{L} or root. Therefore root always reflects ℒ\mathcal{L}. ∎

Corollary 4.1 (Anti-Equivocation).

If two verifiers obtain root1≠root2\mathrm{root}_{1}\neq\mathrm{root}_{2} from the kernel, at least one does not correspond to the kernel’s true log—equivocation is detected. Specifically, for a claimed prefix relation ℒ⊑ℒ′\mathcal{L}\sqsubseteq\mathcal{L}^{\prime}, a consistency proof (Definition 4.10) can verify that ℒ\mathcal{L} is indeed a prefix of ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime}; verification failure proves tampering or forking. Caveat: this property requires at least two independent verifiers comparing roots. In the single-user, single-machine deployment (the current PunkGo scenario), external root anchoring—e.g., periodically publishing roots to a public service or a trusted third party—is needed to realize anti-equivocation in practice. The kernel’s Audit Prover already exports signed tree heads in the C2SP checkpoint format, providing the architectural hook for such anchoring.

Invariant 4.4 (Boundary Enforcement).

∀\forall action AA by actor pp: (𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡⁡(A),𝑡𝑦𝑝𝑒⁡(A))∉W⁡(p)⟹A(\mathit{target}(A),\mathit{type}(A))\notin W(p)\implies A is not committed and produces no log entry.

Proof sketch.

(Step 1) validate is the first pipeline step. Its postcondition: if (𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡⁡(A),𝑡𝑦𝑝𝑒⁡(A))∈W⁡(𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑜𝑟⁡(A))(\mathit{target}(A),\mathit{type}(A))\in W(\mathit{actor}(A)), return Validated; otherwise return Rejected and terminate the pipeline.

(Step 2) The settle and append steps (which commit the action to the permanent log) are reachable only after validate returns Validated.

(Step 3) The Rejected path does not pass through settle or append. The kernel does not record a rejection event in the append-only log (the action never entered the committed pipeline), ensuring no state changes occur.

Design note: Not recording rejections is a deliberate trade-off. Security audit systems (e.g., auditd) typically log failed attempts to detect probing attacks. In PunkGo, the energy system provides an alternative defense: each attempt (including those targeting holds) consumes energy, making sustained probing self-limiting. Optionally logging rejections as zero-cost observe events is a configurable extension that does not affect INV-4’s guarantee.

Therefore out-of-bounds actions cannot be committed. ∎

Invariant 4.5 (Energy Conservation).

∀\forall actor pp, ∀t\forall\,t: E⁡(p,t)≥0E(p,t)\geq 0.

Proof sketch.

(Step 1) quote computes cost⁡(A)\mathrm{cost}(A). reserve checks: E⁡(𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑜𝑟⁡(A))−reserved⁡(𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑜𝑟⁡(A))≥cost⁡(A)E(\mathit{actor}(A))-\mathrm{reserved}(\mathit{actor}(A))\geq\mathrm{cost}(A). If unsatisfied, InsufficientEnergy is returned and AA is not committed.

(Step 2) On successful reservation: reserved+=cost⁡(A)\mathrm{reserved}\mathrel{+}=\mathrm{cost}(A). The sole-committer guarantee (Definition 4.5) ensures no concurrent operation can double-spend the same energy.

(Step 3) settle converts reserved to consumed: E⁡(p)-=actual​_​costE(p)\mathrel{-}=\mathrm{actual\_cost}. For hold reject/timeout: E⁡(p)-=⌈0.2×reserved​_​cost⌉E(p)\mathrel{-}=\lceil 0.2\times\mathrm{reserved\_cost}\rceil. In both cases, the deduction does not exceed the amount verified available at reservation time.

Therefore E⁡(p,t)≥0E(p,t)\geq 0 always holds. ∎

Invariant Dependencies.

The five invariants form a security chain (Figure 1): Boundary Enforcement (INV-4) ensures only legitimate actions enter the pipeline; Energy Conservation (INV-5) ensures legitimate actions have sufficient resources; Completeness (INV-2) ensures every executed or held action is recorded; Append-Only (INV-1) ensures records cannot be tampered with; Integrity (INV-3) ensures tamper-evidence is independently verifiable. Compromising any invariant requires first compromising its upstream invariant.

5 System Design: PunkGo Kernel

5.1 Architecture Overview

Figure 2 illustrates PunkGo’s three-layer architecture.

PunkGo follows a three-layer architecture:

Kernel Layer (TCB).

A Rust user-space process serving as the sole commit point for all AI agent actions. Components: Event Log (Merkle tree), Energy Ledger, Boundary Checker, Payload Validator, and Audit Prover. The kernel is a committer, not an executor: it validates, records, and proves actions, but does not spawn or run external processes on behalf of any actor.

Agent Layer.

Receives commands from the client layer (locally via CLI, or remotely via a messaging protocol such as Matrix) and submits actions to the kernel below. Agents handle LLM reasoning, tool invocation, and execution; they submit action results to the kernel for recording. Agents do not directly manipulate kernel state—all committed records must pass through the kernel pipeline.

Client Layer.

Remote control entry point communicating with agents via a messaging protocol (e.g., Matrix). Provides dashboard, hold-approval interface, and history browser. The client does not interact directly with the kernel.

A key design principle: the kernel is command-source agnostic. Whether a command arrives from a local CLI or a remote messaging protocol does not affect the kernel’s validation, execution, and recording logic, ensuring audit consistency.

5.2 Action Pipeline

The kernel processes each action through its submit_action entry point, a 7-step pipeline:

  1. 1.

    Validate: Check actor existence and active status; verify that the action target falls within the actor’s writable boundary ((𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡,𝑡𝑦𝑝𝑒)∈W⁡(𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑜𝑟))((\mathit{target},\mathit{type})\in W(\mathit{actor})); for state-changing actions, check envelope authorization. [INV-4]

  2. 2.

    Quote: Compute cost⁡(A)\mathrm{cost}(A) via quote_cost.

  3. 3.

    Reserve: Check envelope available energy ≥cost⁡(A)\geq\mathrm{cost}(A) and lock the required amount. [INV-5]

  4. 4.

    Validate Payload: For execute actions, validate that all required fields are present with correct types and that OID format is valid (sha256: followed by 64 hex characters). For other action types, validate the corresponding payload constraints.

  5. 5.

    Settle: Convert locked energy to consumed, finalizing energy accounting.

  6. 6.

    Append: Write the committed event to the append-only log, compute the RFC 6962 leaf hash, update the Merkle tree, and write the audit leaf. [INV-1, INV-3]

  7. 7.

    Receipt: Return a verifiable receipt: event_id (UUID), log_index (sequence number), event_hash (SHA-256).

The pipeline is synchronous, linear, and deterministic—a direct consequence of the sole-committer design. Any step failure terminates the pipeline: validate failure returns Rejected; reserve failure returns InsufficientEnergy. Failed paths produce no log entries.

Hold path.

Hold is not a branch within the pipeline; it is a short-circuit exit inside validate. When validate detects that an action matches the envelope’s hold_on rules, the kernel performs the following operations inside the validate step, within a single database transaction:

  1. 1.

    Call quote_cost to compute the energy cost,

  2. 2.

    Reserve energy on the envelope,

  3. 3.

    Append a hold_request event to the log and audit tree,

  4. 4.

    Create a hold request record,

  5. 5.

    Commit the transaction and return HoldTriggered.

Normal pipeline steps 2–7 are unreachable for held actions. From an abstract perspective, the hold path is: validate​(including quote+reserve+append hold_request)→HoldTriggered\texttt{validate}(\text{including quote}+\text{reserve}+\text{append hold\_request})\to\texttt{HoldTriggered}.

Hold response.

A human responds via mutate ledger/hold/<id>:

Approve. The kernel recursively re-submits the original action to submit_action with two payload markers (replay guards): (1) _hold_approved, which causes the hold-rule check inside validate to become a no-op, and (2) _hold_reserved_cost, which causes quote and reserve to produce a phantom reservation matching the amount locked at hold time, preventing double-charging. The re-submitted action traverses the full pipeline: validate re-checks actor status, boundary permissions, and envelope authorization (which may have changed during the hold period), while steps 4–7 execute normally. This design avoids a special “resume from step 4” path; instead, it reuses the same submit_action function with replay guards that make already-completed steps idempotent.

Reject. Settle commitment cost (⌈0.2×𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑒𝑟𝑣𝑒𝑑​_​𝑐𝑜𝑠𝑡⌉\lceil 0.2\times\mathit{reserved\_cost}\rceil), release remaining energy, and append a hold_response event.

Timeout (if hold_timeout_secs is configured): equivalent to reject.

Figure 3 illustrates the flow.

5.3 Append-Only Event Log

Persistence is backed by a configurable append-only storage backend (the reference implementation uses SQLite in WAL mode, but the design does not bind to any specific database—any store providing atomic writes and durability guarantees is substitutable). The Merkle tree implementation is based on the Google tlog algorithm (C2SP tlog-checkpoint signed tree head format):

  • •

    Leaf nodes: H(0𝚡𝟶𝟶∥𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑛𝑡_𝑑𝑎𝑡𝑎)H(0\mathtt{x00}\|\mathit{event\_data}) (RFC 6962 §2.1)

  • •

    Internal nodes: H⁡(0​𝚡𝟶𝟷​‖𝑙𝑒𝑓𝑡‖​𝑟𝑖𝑔ℎ𝑡)H(0\mathtt{x01}\|\mathit{left}\|\mathit{right})

Two proof types are supported: inclusion proofs (O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n), verifying a specific event’s existence) and consistency proofs (O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n), verifying the old log is a prefix of the new log). Users can export any time range of events plus Merkle proofs as a standalone, independently verifiable audit package.

5.4 Energy Ledger

The energy system anchors hardware compute capacity as a virtual resource:

  • •

    Hardware capacity: Read from a configuration file at startup; runtime hardware probing is future work.

  • •

    Tick production: Energy produced at fixed intervals, recorded in the log.

  • •

    Share allocation: Distributed proportionally among actors.

  • •

    Envelope budgets: Creators allocate budgets to agents, with permissions that cannot exceed the creator’s own.

The 20% commitment cost on rejected or timed-out holds reflects actual resource consumption and deters boundary probing (see §4.5 for the formal rationale).

5.5 Hold/Approval Workflow

Table 2 contrasts PunkGo’s hold mechanism with existing approaches.

PunkGo’s hold is not merely flow control; it is an economic constraint that prevents agents from probing system boundaries via mass hold requests.

5.6 Execute Submission

The kernel is a committer, not an executor. For execute actions, the actor performs the execution externally and submits the result to the kernel. The kernel validates the payload format and records the event—it does not spawn, run, or wait for external processes on behalf of any actor.

The execute payload must contain:

  • •

    input_oid: sha256:<64 hex> — reference to serialized input (command, args, env, working directory)

  • •

    output_oid: sha256:<64 hex> — reference to serialized output (stdout, stderr)

  • •

    exit_code: integer — process exit code

  • •

    artifact_hash: sha256:<64 hex> — SHA-256 of the raw output bytes

  • •

    output_bytes: integer (optional) — output size for IO cost calculation

The kernel validates that all required fields are present with correct types and that OID format is valid, but does not verify whether OID references point to actual content. The kernel records what the actor claims, consistent with mutate behavior. The implications of this trust boundary—and the analogy to Certificate Transparency’s approach—are discussed in §8. Energy cost: 25+⌊𝑜𝑢𝑡𝑝𝑢𝑡​_​𝑏𝑦𝑡𝑒𝑠/256⌋25+\lfloor\mathit{output\_bytes}/256\rfloor.

This design maintains symmetry across all four action types: for mutate, the actor writes files and submits metadata (content_oid); for execute, the actor performs the execution and submits the result. In both cases, the actor acts, the kernel records. Execution environment management (sandboxing, working directory isolation, timeout enforcement) is the actor’s responsibility.

6 Evaluation

PunkGo is evaluated along two dimensions: qualitative invariant verification and quantitative performance characterization. All benchmarks use fresh kernel instances (clean databases) and are compiled with --release optimization.

6.1 Experimental Setup

  • •

    Hardware: Intel Core i7-14700K (14th gen, 20 cores / 28 threads, 32 logical), 64 GB DDR5-5600 RAM, NVMe SSD.

  • •

    Software: Windows 11 Pro (build 26100), PunkGo Kernel v0.2.1, Rust 1.90.0 (release mode), SQLite WAL backend.

  • •

    Code: Open-sourced at https://github.com/PunkGo/punkgo-kernel. Benchmark scripts included in the repository.

  • •

    Methodology: Latency tests use 200 iterations (20 warmup discarded), reporting medians and 95th percentiles. Throughput tests use 5-second windows. All benchmarks are single-threaded (sole-committer design).

6.2 Invariant Verification

Adversarial test scenarios were designed for each invariant. All five pass:

INV-1 (Append-Only).

The test submitted 5 actions, then bypassed the kernel to directly modify the third event’s payload in the underlying store. The recomputed event hash diverged from the stored Merkle leaf hash (f79d... →\to 6a3e...). Inclusion proof verification against the original root: failed (expected). Tamper detection confirmed in 55 ms.

INV-2 (Completeness).

The test submitted 20 actions: 5×\timesobserve, 5×\timescreate, 5×\timesmutate, and 5×\timesout-of-bounds mutate (targeting system/*). All 15 legitimate actions produced event records; 5 violations were rejected at validate (pipeline entry), producing no log entries—correct behavior, as INV-2 covers only boundary-checked actions. Hold mechanism tested separately: both hold_request and hold_response events recorded. 100 ms.

INV-3 (Integrity).

The test submitted 10 actions and generated inclusion proofs for each, verifying with an independent RFC 6962 verifier (not kernel code). All 10/10 passed. Proof lengths matched expectations: ⌈log2⁡(10)⌉=4\lceil\log_{2}(10)\rceil=4 hashes (average 3.6, as trailing leaves have shorter paths). After appending 5 more events, consistency proof (old=10, new=15) verified successfully. 72 ms.

INV-4 (Boundary Enforcement).

The test created an agent with writable_targets restricted to workspace/docs/* (mutate only) and tested 7 scenarios covering: in-bounds access, out-of-bounds target, disallowed action type, privileged targets (system/*, ledger/*), observe exemption, and root override. All 7/7 matched expected behavior. 55 ms.

INV-5 (Energy Conservation).

Envelope with budget=100, cost-per-mutate=15. Six successful mutates (balance: 100→\to85→\to70→\to55→\to40→\to25→\to10); seventh rejected with InsufficientEnergy, balance unchanged at 10. Hold commitment test: budget=1000, hold reserved=15, reject settled ⌈15×0.2⌉=3\lceil 15\times 0.2\rceil=3, balance 1000→9971000\to 997. Balance never negative. 96 ms.

6.3 Performance Characteristics

Action Pipeline Latency.

End-to-end latency encompasses the full pipeline (validate through receipt, plus post-commit audit checkpoint). Table 3 reports results over 200 iterations.

Median latency is 0.7–1.3 ms per action, dominated by storage I/O (event persistence and Merkle tree update). The execute action type adds a validate_payload step (OID format checking) but exhibits latency comparable to mutate, confirming that payload validation adds negligible overhead. Medians and percentiles are reported rather than means with error bars because latency distributions are right-skewed; percentiles better characterize tail behavior.

Merkle Proof Scaling.

Table 4 shows inclusion proof generation time and size as the log grows.

Proof size (hash count) follows O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) precisely: from 4 hashes at 10 entries to 14 hashes at 10,000 (⌈log2⁡10,000⌉=14\lceil\log_{2}10{,}000\rceil=14). Each hash is 32 bytes (SHA-256), so a 10,000-entry proof is only 448 bytes. Generation time grows as O⁡(n)O(n) because the current implementation loads all hash nodes from storage before computing the O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) proof path—an engineering optimization opportunity (paginated loading would restore O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) time). At 10,000 entries, proof generation takes ∼\sim19 ms; 100,000-entry benchmarks were attempted but the O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) cumulative fill cost (each commit triggers O⁡(n)O(n) hash loading) made the test impractical, confirming that the hash-loading optimization is the critical scaling bottleneck.

Throughput.

Table 5 reports sequential single-committer throughput over 5-second windows.

Throughput is ∼\sim390–450 actions/sec. The bottleneck is storage I/O (event persistence and Merkle checkpoint). For personal AI agent usage (typical daily volume in the hundreds to low thousands), current throughput is sufficient.

Hold Workflow Latency.

Table 6 reports mechanical latency only, excluding human decision time.

Sample size is small (n=8n=8) because each hold test requires multi-step setup (envelope creation, hold trigger, human-response simulation); the table reports medians and maxima rather than percentiles. End-to-end mechanical latency (trigger to approve completion): ∼\sim3.0 ms. Approve is ∼\sim2×\times slower than reject because it re-submits the original action through the full pipeline and writes two events (action result + hold response), whereas reject only settles commitment cost and writes one event.

6.4 Comparison with AIOS

Table 7 provides a qualitative capability comparison between PunkGo and AIOS [2], the leading agent operating system. Direct latency comparison is not meaningful: AIOS includes LLM inference and tool execution in its critical path, whereas PunkGo’s kernel measures only the commit path (validate through append). The two systems occupy different layers of the stack.

7 Related Work

AI Agent Governance.

Agent Contracts [1] formalizes a contract framework C=(I,O,S,R,T,Φ,Ψ)C=(I,O,S,R,T,\Phi,\Psi) for resource-bounded agents, achieving 90% token savings. Contracts define what agents may do; PunkGo records what they actually did—the two are complementary. Infrastructure for AI Agents [15] proposes agent identity and attribution infrastructure but targets inter-agent interaction, not user-side verification on personal hardware. OpenAI Governance Practices [16] enumerates seven desirable properties (readability, monitoring, attributability, interruptibility, etc.) that presuppose persistent recording infrastructure but do not specify one.

Agent Access Control.

AgentSentry [6] generates minimal ephemeral permissions; AgentBound [17] provides MCP access control. Both enforce policy at invocation time but neither produces persistent tamper-evident records of what was actually executed.

Transparent Logs and Verifiable Data Structures.

Certificate Transparency [3] established the canonical Merkle tree append-only log paradigm. Crosby and Wallach [9] formalized tamper-evident log data structure semantics. A2M [10] embeds an append-only primitive in the TCB—the PunkGo kernel serves an analogous architectural role but targets AI agents rather than Byzantine consensus. CONIKS [8] extended transparent logs to end-user key verification. Google’s Trillian [32] provides engineering-scale validation of the paradigm across multiple applications. PunkGo applies this transparent log paradigm to a new domain: OS-level AI agent action auditing on personal hardware.

OS-Level Audit Systems.

The Linux Audit Framework (auditd) [25] provides kernel-level syscall logging with configurable filtering rules and is widely deployed for compliance auditing (e.g., CAPP/EAL4+). However, auditd operates at the syscall granularity, not the agent-action level: it records open(), write(), execve() but cannot attribute these syscalls to a specific agent’s semantic action (e.g., “agent X modified document Y under envelope Z”). It also provides no cryptographic tamper evidence—logs are plain-text files that a root user can silently edit. Windows Event Tracing (ETW) shares these limitations. PunkGo operates at a higher semantic level (agent actions rather than syscalls) and provides Merkle-based tamper evidence that auditd lacks.

eBPF-Based Runtime Auditing.

eBPF [36] extends the Linux kernel with sandboxed programs that attach to syscall and kernel events, enabling flexible runtime tracing and policy enforcement without kernel modification. Falco [37] applies eBPF to container runtime security; AgentCgroup [20] applies eBPF and cgroups to characterize AI agent resource dynamics. These tools operate at the syscall granularity—they observe open(), execve(), and cgroup counters, but cannot attribute syscall sequences to agent-level semantic actions or produce cryptographic tamper evidence. eBPF programs must terminate in bounded steps and cannot block for asynchronous human decisions, precluding mechanisms like PunkGo’s hold workflow. Furthermore, eBPF is Linux-specific; PunkGo’s user-space design is cross-platform by construction. The two approaches are complementary: eBPF provides fine-grained OS-level resource traces that could cross-validate agent-declared actions at the semantic layer.

Blockchain-Based Audit.

Permissioned blockchains such as Hyperledger Fabric [26] provide tamper-evident distributed ledgers with ordering-service consensus, achieving 3,500+ tx/sec in multi-peer deployments. However, blockchain-based audit imposes significant architectural overhead for single-machine AI agent logging: Fabric requires multi-node consensus (even in crash-fault-tolerant mode), introduces network latency, and demands infrastructure far exceeding a personal workstation. For the target scenario—personal AI agents on local hardware—the trust model requires protecting a single user’s history from untrusted agents, not achieving consensus among mutually distrusting organizations. PunkGo adopts the cryptographic structure (Merkle trees) without the consensus overhead.

TEE-Based Attestation.

Graphene-SGX (now Gramine) [27] demonstrates that unmodified applications can run inside Intel SGX enclaves with modest overhead, providing confidentiality and integrity against a malicious OS. TEE-based execution is complementary to PunkGo: running the kernel inside an SGX/TDX enclave would elevate tamper-evidence guarantees from Level 1 (untrusted agents) to Level 2 (privileged platform adversaries), as discussed in §3. This integration is listed as future work.

OS-Level Security and Formal Verification.

seL4 [4] proved OS kernel functional correctness and capability isolation—but seL4 proves what agents cannot do; it does not record what they did. Capsicum [18] brought practical capability security to UNIX—but without history recording. CertiKOS [38] extends verified kernel construction to concurrent settings with compositional layered specifications. IronFleet [19]’s three-layer refinement verification methodology (TLA+-style specification →\to protocol layer →\to implementation) serves as the template for PunkGo’s formalization approach. AgentCgroup [20] first characterized OS-level resource dynamics of AI agents—but without a security model or audit mechanism. Verus [13] provides a Rust verification framework and is the target tool for PunkGo’s future machine-checked proofs.

Agent Operating Systems.

AIOS [2] is the leading agent OS, providing scheduling, context management, and basic access control with 2.1×\times faster agent execution. Its access control uses a permission-group hashmap—functional for resource management but without audit logging, Merkle evidence, or capability-based isolation. The companion vision paper [21] positions the LLM as an OS-level scheduler and resource manager. The characterization of “LLM as TCB” in Table 7 reflects the observation that AIOS’s security boundary does not extend below the LLM scheduling layer, not a claim that AIOS deliberately places security trust in LLMs. The two systems address complementary concerns: AIOS optimizes agent execution; PunkGo provides verifiable action recording.

Human Oversight and AI Safety.

The Off-Switch Game [22] proves utility-maximizing agents are incentivized to disable human intervention. Corrigibility [23] formalizes cooperation with correction. The Oversight Game [24] models oversight as a dynamic Markov game. These works establish theoretical foundations but lack implementation infrastructure—specifically, a verifiable record of when humans oversaw, what they decided, and whether agents complied. PunkGo’s hold mechanism and its Merkle-logged events are precisely the infrastructure these theoretical models assume but do not specify.

Sovereignty and Local-First.

Local-First Software [11] establishes data ownership principles. Solid [12] provides data storage location control. Sovereign Agents [5] analyzes how agents maintain sovereignty from humans. This paper argues the question points in the wrong direction: in the context of AI agents acting on behalf of humans, what requires protection is human sovereignty over agents. The Right to History extends local-first principles from data ownership to computational history ownership.

Data Provenance and Trust.

Provenance in databases [35] provides formal foundations for tracking the origin and transformation of data. Trust and reputation models for multi-agent systems [34] establish frameworks for evaluating agent behavior based on historical records. PunkGo provides the infrastructure layer that such provenance and trust systems require: a tamper-evident, independently verifiable record of agent actions, upon which provenance queries and reputation assessments can be built.

8 Discussion and Future Work

Limitations.

(1) The current design uses a single-node, single-committer architecture with no multi-writer concurrency. This is deliberate: single-point linearization yields a deterministic total-order log, avoiding consensus protocol complexity. Distributed extension requires introducing consensus (e.g., Raft) and re-proving invariants under multi-committer semantics. (2) Formal arguments are structured proof sketches, not machine-checked. (3) Merkle proof generation exhibits O⁡(n)O(n) time due to loading all hash nodes from storage before computing the O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) proof path. At 10,000 entries proof generation takes ∼\sim19 ms; an attempted 100,000-entry benchmark was impractical due to O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) cumulative fill cost (each commit triggers O⁡(n)O(n) hash loading). Paginated or incremental hash loading would restore O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) generation time and is the critical scaling optimization. (4) The threat model assumes kernel code is trusted. (5) Throughput of ∼\sim400 actions/sec is sufficient for personal agent usage but is bottlenecked by per-commit storage I/O (event persistence and Merkle checkpoint); batched commits or write-ahead buffering could improve throughput for higher-volume scenarios. (6) Hardware compute detection (INT8 TOPS) is currently configuration-file only; runtime probing is not implemented. (7) Execution environment isolation is the actor’s responsibility; the kernel provides recording but not execution containment. Reference sandbox implementations for actors are future work.

Privacy Considerations and the Right to Erasure.

An append-only action log creates an inherent tension with the right to erasure under data protection regulations [30]. Three mitigating factors apply. First, in the primary deployment scenario—personal hardware, single user—the data controller and data subject are the same person; self-processing falls outside the material scope of most data protection frameworks (e.g., GDPR’s household exemption). Second, for organizational deployments, the architecture supports crypto-erasure: log entries can be encrypted with per-entity keys, and key destruction renders ciphertext unrecoverable while preserving the Merkle tree’s structural integrity (hash nodes commit to ciphertext, not plaintext). Implementation of crypto-erasure is future work. Third, for high-risk AI systems, regulatory logging mandates (e.g., EU AI Act Article 12 [28]) may create a legal basis that overrides erasure requests. A complete legal analysis of this interplay is beyond the scope of this paper.

Trust Boundary of Action Recording.

The kernel records what agents claim to have done, not necessarily what actually happened in the external world. For the execute action type, the actor performs the execution externally and submits a structured payload (input/output OIDs, exit code, artifact hash). The kernel validates payload format and OID syntax, but does not verify whether OID references point to actual content or whether declared results correspond to actual execution outcomes. This is an explicit design choice, analogous to Certificate Transparency: CT log servers record that a Certificate Authority claims to have issued a certificate, without verifying the certificate’s content correctness [3]. The value lies in the tamper-evident attribution record—who claimed what, when, under what authorization—which supports after-the-fact audit and dispute resolution. For use cases requiring stronger guarantees (e.g., verifying that an agent’s declared file modification matches the actual file state), content verification at the actor’s execution environment can be added as an extension without modifying the kernel.

Future Work.

(1) Machine-checked verification: End-to-end proofs from TLA+ specification to Rust code using Verus [13]. (2) TEE integration: Running the kernel inside Intel SGX/TDX to reduce trust assumptions. (3) Multi-agent collaboration: A2A protocol integration for multi-agent scenarios. (4) External tool ecosystem: Modern AI agent frameworks increasingly adopt standardized tool-lifecycle protocols (e.g., MCP) that allow agents to discover, invoke, and manage external tools automatically. Integrating such protocols would enable PunkGo to record tool invocations as auditable execute events, bridging the gap between automated tool orchestration and verifiable action history. (5) Cross-organization verification: A public Merkle proof verification service analogous to CT log servers. (6) Performance optimization: Paginated or incremental hash loading for Merkle proof generation (eliminating O⁡(n)O(n) proof-time overhead) and batched commit modes for higher throughput. (7) Actor-side execution isolation: Reference sandbox implementations (Docker, Firecracker microVM) for actors to use before submitting execute results to the kernel. (8) Syscall-level cross-validation: On Linux, eBPF-based syscall tracing [36] could cross-validate agent-declared actions against actual system call sequences, though this requires a semantic-to-syscall attribution model that is an independent research problem. (9) Hardware probing: Runtime INT8 TOPS auto-detection replacing configuration files.

9 Conclusion

As AI agents increasingly act on behalf of humans, a fundamental question emerges: who records what happened? This paper defines the Right to History—the principle that individuals are entitled to a complete, verifiable, tamper-evident record of every AI agent action—and provides a formal framework to realize it. The paper argues five system invariants (Append-Only, Completeness, Integrity, Boundary Enforcement, and Energy Conservation) via structured proof sketches, forming a security chain from behavior isolation to verifiable auditing. The PunkGo Kernel implements this framework as a Rust sovereignty kernel, unifying the cryptographic auditing of Certificate Transparency, the capability isolation spirit of seL4, and an energy governance model into one system. Evaluation confirms all invariants hold under adversarial testing, with sub-1.3 ms action latency and logarithmic-size Merkle proofs.

The Right to History is not an optional feature layered atop an existing system; it is a foundational architectural commitment—the event log and its invariants determine the system’s structure, not the reverse. PunkGo aims to encourage the systems community to treat verifiable action recording as a first-class concern in AI agent infrastructure.

Data and Code Availability.

The PunkGo Kernel source code, benchmark scripts, and all raw benchmark data reported in this paper are available at https://github.com/PunkGo/punkgo-kernel under the MIT License. Project homepage: https://punkgo.ai.
